title: The 2027 Mark Palmer Prize: Call for Nominations
content:
Freedom House is now accepting nominations for the 2027 Mark Palmer Prize, inviting individuals and organizations around the world to put forward candidates whose work exemplifies the important role of diplomacy in supporting democratic movements and defending fundamental freedoms.

The award takes its name from the late Mark Palmer, a longtime Freedom House trustee and US ambassador to Hungary from 1986 to 1990. In 1989, as the Cold War was coming to a close, Palmer boldly joined civil society and the Hungarian democratic opposition to support the country’s transition to democracy.
 
The Mark Palmer Prize has been awarded to diplomats and international civil servants from around the world, including Georgia, Peru, the Czech Republic, Lithuania, Mongolia, Sweden, Canada, Uruguay, and the United States. The prize is made possible through the generosity of the Mark and Sushma Palmer Legacy Fund, established by Dr. Sushma Palmer in loving memory of her late husband and former Freedom House trustee and vice chairman Ambassador Mark Palmer. 

Nomination Form

Criteria 

The award winner must be a current or former diplomat or official serving in an intergovernmental institution.

title: Nicaragua’s Future: Repression, Resistance, and Hope
content:
Register


Over the past two decades, Nicaragua has experienced one of the world's most dramatic declines in freedom, losing 49 points on Freedom in the World’s 100-point scale assessing political rights and civil liberties. The regime of Daniel Ortega and his wife and “co-president” Rosario Murillo has systematically dismantled democratic institutions, imprisoned political opponents, killed peaceful protestors, and shuttered thousands of civil society organizations, independent media outlets, and religious institutions. Moreover, it has exported its repression beyond Nicaragua's borders, targeting dissidents in neighboring Costa Rica with surveillance, intimidation, and violence. The regime has also deepened its cooperation with other authoritarian powers, including those ruling China, Cuba, Russia, and Iran.

title: After the Election: Revitalizing Serbian Democracy, and Lessons from the Opposition Victory
content:
Sun shining through a Serbian flag. (Photo Credit: Ivan Radic on Flickr CC BY 2.0)

Last month Serbia’s Student List, a youth-backed opposition movement, won parliamentary elections, ending 14 years of rule by longtime Serbian leader Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). The broad coalition grew from an ongoing protest movement sparked by the collapse of a renovated canopy at Novi Sad’s train station in 2024, which killed more than a dozen people and was widely blamed on government corruption.

Political rights and civil liberties had eroded significantly under Vučić’s rule as the government placed legal and extralegal pressure on the political opposition, independent media, and civil society organizations. As a result, Serbia’s Freedom in the World status declined from Free to Partly Free in 2019. Its score has since continued to decline, now registering 53 points on Freedom in the World’s 100-point scale—the lowest score in the western Balkan region and the second-lowest score in all of Europe. Turnout in the election was reported at a massive 70 percent, reflecting Serbian citizens’ desire for reforms in their country.

title: The Cuban Regime Didn't Just Interrupt a UN Event. It Validated Its Own Central Premise.
content:
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz reacts to Cuban diplomats following the Cuba Libre event. (Photo Credit: US Mission to the United Nations)

At a United Nations event last week, the Cuban regime proved its critics right.

On October 19, diplomats, UN officials, and journalists gathered in New York to hear directly from brave Cubans whose lives have been shaped by political imprisonment, censorship, forced exile, and repression. They came to discuss what happens in Cuba when citizens peacefully exercise their fundamental rights.

By the end of the event, they had their answer.

What unfolded at the United Nations was instantly recognizable to many Cubans. Cuba's permanent representative to the UN, Ernesto Soberón Guzmán, and other government representatives crowded the entrances and hallways outside the meeting room, filming attendees, including the organizer, US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz, shouting accusations and branding regime critics “terrorists” and “liars.” The scene mirrored the harassment and smear campaigns that the regime has long deployed against its opponents.

title: Family Members Speak: The Toll of Political Imprisonment
content:
In his final public statement, Chinese Nobel Peace Prize laureate Liu Xiaobo wrote to his wife: “I am serving my sentence in a tangible prison, while you wait in the intangible prison of the heart.” His words capture the often-overlooked suffering of families who grapple with emotional anguish, mounting legal fees, and fears for their loved ones’ health and safety. Many find themselves thrust into the unfamiliar role of advocate, fighting for due process, visitation rights, and even basic information about those held incommunicado.

Solidarity with political prisoners must also extend to the families who endure these hardships. Below, they share their experiences in their own words.

Talia Khattak, daughter of political prisoner Idris Khattak

Every morning I wake up and try to carry on with my life, and every night the constant worry returns, and my heart drops: my father was convicted in a fake trial, he is getting old and sick, and he is not receiving his medicine. I lie awake wondering if he is in pain, if he knows how hard we are fighting for him. I should be caring for him now, yet I can’t hear his voice telling me it’s going to be okay.

title: A Message from the Founding Families: Carrying the Torch Forward
content:
Eighty-five years ago, in 1941, totalitarian forces were aggressively advancing across the world. To address this challenge, First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt and Wendell Willkie, her husband’s Republican opponent in the previous election, came together to lead the formation of Freedom House, a philosophically and professionally diverse group of prominent citizens committed to the cause of liberty. At that pivotal moment in American history, when isolationism was prevalent, Roosevelt and Willkie set aside partisan differences in the shared belief that American leadership would be essential in the approaching global struggle for freedom.

And indeed, it was. After World War II, when Nazi Germany and its aligned powers were vanquished and Soviet communism emerged as a new totalitarian threat, Freedom House campaigned for the institutions and ideals that defined the modern democratic order, including the Marshall Plan, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and the NATO alliance. The organization also worked to advance the realization of the United States’ own democratic ideals, standing in steadfast opposition to McCarthyism and joining the fight for civil rights for all Americans.

title: TNR Watch: The Enduring Problem of Transnational Repression in Southeast Asia
content:
Déjà vu: Two apparent incidents of transnational repression (TNR) endangered several diaspora activists in Southeast Asia in mid-September. On September 15, Khieo Lapchanh, a Thailand-based Laotian asylum seeker known for his online criticism of Laos’s government, went missing outside Bangkok. The 26-year-old, who was set to attend an asylum interview at the UN Refugee agency office in Bangkok a day later, reportedly was the target of an $8,000 bounty circulating online.

Three days after Lapchanh’s disappearance, three Vietnamese activists—Nguyen Duc Thuan, Ho Pham Hiep Huy, and Thai Cong Truong Son—were abducted from Cambodia and returned to Vietnam, where they are under investigation for “terrorism” and forging documents. Australian resident Hiep and dual Norwegian-Vietnamese citizen Thuan went to Cambodia to meet and train other Vietnamese human rights defenders. According to the prodemocracy organization Viet Tan, which Hiep and Thuan belong to, Vietnamese authorities initially prevented consular visits by Australian and Norwegian representatives to the two while they were in detention.

title: NEW REPORT: Authoritarian Internet Controls Drive 16th Consecutive Year of Decline in Global Internet Freedom
content:
WASHINGTON, DC—Global internet freedom declined for the 16th consecutive year, with conditions deteriorating in 16 of the 38 countries assessed and improving in only 8, according to Freedom on the Net 2026: Seismic Shifts on the Global Internet, a new report released today by Freedom House. Authoritarian efforts to isolate populations from the global internet, expanding age checks for online access, and the weaponization of laws governing AI-generated content created new barriers to free expression and access to information. 

“Agentic AI promises to transform the internet,” said Freedom House Chief Executive Officer Jamie Fly. “Authoritarian actors are already weaponizing AI. We need to ensure that frontline activists and freedom fighters have access to cutting-edge technologies to counter these threats and to accelerate freedom in repressive societies. Democracies need to ensure that efforts to secure democracy and fundamental rights in the AI era do not restrict legitimate expression.”

title: Update from Freedom House CEO Jamie Fly: New Partnerships and Opportunities to Stand for Freedom
content:
This fall brought new partnerships and new opportunities to stand with those on the front lines of the fight for freedom.

Carnegie Council for Ethics in International Affairs

In September, I joined Carnegie Council President Joel Rosenthal in New York for Carnegie’s Values and Interests series. We discussed why democracy is both a moral and a political principle, the regression of freedom globally, and what can be done to counter the new wave of autocrats and illiberal actors.

title: Joint Statement for the International Day of Political Prisoners on October 30
content:
The October 30 Coalition have released the following joint statement to rally support for political prisoners and champion their freedom. The joint statement highlights the importance of sustained international attention to individual political prisoners, efforts to secure their release, and accountability for abuses. The October 30 Coalition consists of the 30 October Foundation, Free Russia Foundation, Free Them One by One, Freedom House, the Human Rights Foundation, the Lantos Foundation, the McCain Institute, the National Endowment for Democracy, the Raoul Wallenberg Centre for Human Rights, and World Liberty Congress. Organizations interested in signing the joint statement can fill out this form.

Joint Statement for the International Day of Political Prisoners on October 30

On this International Day of Political Prisoners, we stand together to affirm a simple truth: no one should be imprisoned for speaking freely, standing up for their beliefs, or exercising their fundamental rights.
